a.entradas.erra-ishum.titulo_alternativo: The "weapons of terror": a nuclear war in 2024 BC
a.entradas.erra-ishum.interpretacion: In The Wars of Gods and Men (1985), Sitchin reads the Poem of Erra and Ishum and the laments over the destruction of Ur and Sumer as chronicles of a war between factions of the Anunnaki. The "seven weapons of terror" that Erra (Nergal) and Ishum (for Sitchin, Ninurta) unleash would be nuclear bombs. With them the spaceport in Sinai and the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah would have been destroyed. The "evil wind" of the laments would be the radioactive cloud that, carried east by the prevailing winds, depopulated Sumer. Sitchin dates the event to 2024 BC and considers it the cause of the end of the Third Dynasty of Ur.
a.entradas.erra-ishum.afirmaciones.0.afi: Sitchin: Erra's "seven weapons" are nuclear weapons.
a.entradas.erra-ishum.afirmaciones.0.rep: In the poem, the Seven (Sebettu) are personified warrior demons in the service of Erra, god of plague and war. The devastation it describes, with civil war, epidemics and abandoned cities, matches known calamities of the 1st millennium BC. The text is usually dated to the 9th or 8th century BC, more than a thousand years after Sitchin's date.
a.entradas.erra-ishum.afirmaciones.0.fue: L. Cagni, The Poem of Erra, 1977; B. R. Foster, Before the Muses, 2005
a.entradas.erra-ishum.afirmaciones.1.afi: Sitchin: the "evil wind" of the laments over Ur is the radioactive fallout of a nuclear explosion.
a.entradas.erra-ishum.afirmaciones.1.rep: In the laments, Enlil's "storm" is a metaphor for divine wrath embodied in the invasion of Elamites and people from Shimashki and the political collapse of Ur III around 2004 BC (Middle Chronology). The excavations at Ur show no layer of vitrification or radioactivity.
a.entradas.erra-ishum.afirmaciones.1.fue: P. Michalowski, The Lamentation over the Destruction of Sumer and Ur, 1989
a.entradas.erra-ishum.veredicto: Erra and Ishum is a theological poem about divine wrath and the restoration of order; the nuclear reading projects 20th-century experiences onto metaphorical language.
a.entradas.gilgamesh.titulo_alternativo: Gilgamesh, the demigod who sought the spaceport
a.entradas.gilgamesh.interpretacion: Von Däniken (Chariots of the Gods?, 1968) saw in the Epic of Gilgamesh descriptions of flights and of the effects of acceleration, and in Utnapishtim's Flood a memory of extraterrestrial intervention. Sitchin (The Stairway to Heaven, 1980) interprets Gilgamesh's quest for immortality as a journey to the Anunnaki's "Landing Place" in the Cedar Forest, which he locates at Baalbek (Lebanon), and to the spaceport in Sinai. Gilgamesh's condition as "two-thirds god" would be that of a genetic hybrid. Ancient Aliens takes up these ideas, including the notion that the ark was a spaceship.
a.entradas.gilgamesh.afirmaciones.0.afir: Sitchin: Gilgamesh's Cedar Forest is a landing platform at Baalbek.
a.entradas.gilgamesh.afirmaciones.0.repl: The epic mentions no platforms or launches. The great platform at Baalbek and its blocks (the largest weighing about 800 tons) belong to the Roman temple of Jupiter Heliopolitanus. Colavito points out that the idea of Baalbek as a spaceport did not originate with Sitchin: it was proposed earlier by the Soviet writer Matest M. Agrest.
a.entradas.gilgamesh.afirmaciones.0.fuen: Jason Colavito, "Why ancient astronaut theorists think Gilgamesh visited a rocket launch pad at Baalbek", jasoncolavito.com; Skeptoid no. 720 (Brian Dunning, 2020)
a.entradas.gilgamesh.afirmaciones.1.afir: Ancient Aliens: Gilgamesh's "two-thirds divine" nature proves a hybrid lineage with the Anunnaki.
a.entradas.gilgamesh.afirmaciones.1.repl: The formula expresses the king's mythical parentage, as son of the goddess Ninsun and the hero Lugalbanda, a common royal ideology. Colavito stresses that it has no connection with the Anunnaki or with the Watchers of the Book of Enoch.
a.entradas.gilgamesh.afirmaciones.1.fuen: A. R. George, The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic, 2003; Jason Colavito, review of Ancient Aliens S6E03
a.entradas.gilgamesh.veredicto: The Epic of Gilgamesh is a literary work about death and human limits; the "technical" passages attributed to it do not appear in the text or are poetic images.
a.entradas.diluvio-ziusudra.titulo_alter: The Flood caused by the passage of Nibiru
a.entradas.diluvio-ziusudra.interpretaci: Sitchin (The 12th Planet) maintains that some 13,000 years ago the passage of Nibiru destabilized the Antarctic ice sheet, which slid into the ocean and caused a gigantic wave: the Flood of Ziusudra, Atrahasis and Utnapishtim. The Anunnaki knew and decided not to warn humans, but Enki broke the oath and warned his protégé to build a submersible vessel. The gods would have watched the catastrophe from orbit, "cowering like dogs", in their spacecraft. Ancient Aliens adds that the ark may have been a spaceship, an idea David Childress takes from Bruce Rux (1996).
a.entradas.diluvio-ziusudra.afirmaciones: Sitchin: the Flood was a slide of Antarctic ice caused by Nibiru some 13,000 years ago.

There is no geological evidence of an Antarctic collapse or a global flood at that date, and Nibiru does not exist as a planet. The Mesopotamian Flood stories derive from local river floods in southern Mesopotamia. Moreover, the ark tablet studied by Finkel describes a round reed boat, a coracle, not a technical vessel.
Irving Finkel, The Ark Before Noah, 2014; Lambert and Millard, 1969
Sitchin: the gods "cowering like dogs" were watching from spacecraft in orbit.

The line in Gilgamesh XI says that the gods, terrified, went up to the heaven of Anu and curled up like dogs against the wall. It is an image of divine cowardice consistent with a cosmology in which heaven is the physical place of the gods, and there is no technical vocabulary.
A. R. George, The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic, 2003
a.entradas.diluvio-ziusudra.veredicto: The Mesopotamian Flood is a literary tradition with several versions; the explanation involving Nibiru and Antarctic ice has no geological or textual basis.
a.entradas.adapa.titulo_alternativo: Adapa, the human taken to Anu's ship
a.entradas.adapa.interpretacion: In the myth of Adapa, this sage of Eridu breaks the wing of the South Wind and is summoned before Anu in heaven. Enki advises him to refuse the bread and water he is offered, because they would be "of death", but in fact they were "of life", and Adapa loses immortality. Sitchin interprets this as a human's journey to Nibiru or to an Anunnaki ship, and the "bread and water of life" as foods or treatments that gave the gods their longevity.
a.entradas.adapa.afirmaciones.0.afirmaci: Sitchin: Adapa's ascent to Anu's heaven is a space journey to Nibiru.
a.entradas.adapa.afirmaciones.0.replica: Anu's heaven is the upper level of Mesopotamian cosmology, reached through its "gate", guarded by Dumuzi and Gishzida. The myth explains human mortality through a misunderstanding, a theme analogous to that of Genesis 3, and mentions no vehicle. In other traditions, Adapa is one of the apkallu.
a.entradas.adapa.afirmaciones.0.fuente_r: S. Izre'el, Adapa and the South Wind, 2001
a.entradas.adapa.veredicto: Adapa is a myth about the loss of immortality; the space-journey reading has no support in the text.
a.entradas.anzu.titulo_alternativo: Anzu and the theft of the flight-control data
a.entradas.anzu.interpretacion: Sitchin interprets the Duranki of Nippur, the "bond of heaven and earth", as Enlil's mission control center. The Tablet of Destinies stolen by the bird Anzu (Zu) would contain the colony's orbital and communications data, and its theft would have paralyzed operations until Ninurta recovered it in an aerial battle. Anzu's wings and flight would be those of a spacecraft.
a.entradas.anzu.afirmaciones.0.afirmacio: Sitchin: the Tablet of Destinies is a control device and the Duranki a mission control center.
a.entradas.anzu.afirmaciones.0.replica: The Tablet of Destinies is a symbol of the supreme power to decree destiny (šīmtu), which also appears in the Enuma Elish in Kingu's hands. Duranki is a poetic name for Nippur as the axis between heaven and earth. Anzu is a lion-headed storm bird, well represented in iconography.
a.entradas.anzu.afirmaciones.0.fuente_re: Heiser, sitchiniswrong.com (on the technical equivalents Sitchin invents); B. R. Foster, Before the Muses, 2005
a.entradas.anzu.veredicto: The myth of Anzu deals with cosmic order and Ninurta's legitimacy; the technological reading has no textual basis (Sitchin's reading is documented mainly in secondary sources).
a.entradas.lugal-e.interpretacion: In The Wars of Gods and Men (1985), Sitchin uses the Sumerian poem Lugal-e, in which Ninurta defeats the monster Asag and judges one by one the stones that fought on his side or against him, as a chronicle of a war between factions of the Anunnaki in Egypt. Ninurta would have stormed the Great Pyramid of Giza, which would be a guidance beacon for landings, and the "stones" judged would be crystals and equipment inside it, removed or destroyed.
a.entradas.lugal-e.afirmaciones.0.afirma: Sitchin: the stones Ninurta judges are the equipment of the Great Pyramid.
a.entradas.lugal-e.afirmaciones.0.replic: Lugal-e is an etiological poem that explains the properties and uses of the stones that reached Mesopotamia from the mountains, and why some are used for statues while others are trodden underfoot. No passage mentions Egypt or pyramids. The Great Pyramid is a royal tomb of the 4th Dynasty, unrelated to the Sumerian texts.
a.entradas.lugal-e.afirmaciones.0.fuente: J. van Dijk, LUGAL UD ME-LÁM-bi NIR-ĞÁL, 1983; ETCSL 1.6.2
a.entradas.lugal-e.veredicto: Lugal-e is a myth about the ordering of the mineral world; its transfer to Egypt is Sitchin's construction (a reading documented mainly in secondary summaries).
a.entradas.inanna-enki-me.interpretacion: In the Sumerian myth of Inanna and Enki, the goddess gets Enki drunk and carries off to Uruk the me, more than a hundred "powers" on which civilization rests, in her "boat of heaven". Sitchin interprets the me as technological objects, disks or programs containing the knowledge of civilization, and the boat of heaven as an aircraft, so that the myth would be a transfer of technology from Eridu to Uruk.
a.entradas.inanna-enki-me.afirmaciones.0: Sitchin: the me are technological equipment or programs, and the "boat of heaven" a spacecraft.

The myth's own list of the me, of which some 94 entries survive, includes kingship, priesthood, truth, descent to the Underworld, sacred prostitution, the craft of woodworking, deceit and joy: concepts, crafts and cultural norms. Specialists define them as cosmic and cultural norms or prerogatives. The "boat of heaven" (má-an-na) is Inanna's divine boat, which in the narrative sails along the river.
Michael S. Heiser, sitchiniswrong.com (citing G. Farber and The Context of Scripture, vol. 1); ETCSL 1.3.1
a.entradas.inanna-enki-me.veredicto: The myth explains the prestige of Uruk and of Inanna as keeper of the foundations of civilization; the me are concepts, not devices.
a.entradas.me.titulo_alternativo: The me, the technology of the gods
a.entradas.me.interpretacion: For Sitchin, the me were physical objects containing the knowledge of civilization, something like memory devices. In his books he also links them with the gods' flight equipment: the SHU.GAR.RA headdress would be a space helmet, and the me accessories of the pilots of the "sky chambers". In ancient astronaut culture the me are often described as "chips" or "programs" that the gods gave to kings.
a.entradas.me.afirmaciones.0.afirmacion: Sitchin: SHU.GAR.RA is a space helmet and the me are spaceflight equipment.
a.entradas.me.afirmaciones.0.replica: The statues Sitchin cites show ceremonial headdresses, not helmets. In Inanna and Enki the me are abstract ideas, activities and insignia, and none is linked with flight. The flight reading in turn depends on MU being a spacecraft, something the sources do not support.
a.entradas.me.afirmaciones.0.fuente_repl: Michael S. Heiser, "Zecharia Sitchin's Errors", sitchiniswrong.com; G. Farber, "me", Reallexikon der Assyriologie 7
a.entradas.me.veredicto: The me are a Sumerian theological concept, the norms and powers that make civilization possible; there is no textual evidence that they were artifacts.
a.entradas.zigurat.titulo_alternativo: Ziggurats: control towers and landing platforms
a.entradas.zigurat.interpretacion: Sitchin interprets the Mesopotamian stepped towers as Anunnaki installations: beacons, communication towers or landing platforms for their "sky chambers". In The 12th Planet he reads the shem of the Tower of Babel (Genesis 11) and the Sumerian MU as a conical object "that rises straight up", a rocket, so that the Tower of Babel would be a launch pad. Ancient Aliens and other authors present ziggurats as replicas of ancient flight installations.
a.entradas.zigurat.afirmaciones.0.afirma: Sitchin: MU and the Hebrew shem mean "rocket" or "object that rises", and the Tower of Babel was a launch ramp.
a.entradas.zigurat.afirmaciones.0.replic: Sitchin cites no dictionary. The lexical lists define šamû as "sky" and "rain"; Akkadian šumu and Hebrew shem mean "name" or "fame" (Chicago Assyrian Dictionary). In Genesis 11, the builders raise a city and a tower of brick and bitumen to "make a name" for themselves.
a.entradas.zigurat.afirmaciones.0.fuente: Michael S. Heiser, sitchiniswrong.com (citing W. Horowitz and J. L. Hayes, A Manual of Sumerian Grammar)
a.entradas.zigurat.afirmaciones.1.afirma: Ancient Aliens: ziggurats are landing platforms for the gods.
a.entradas.zigurat.afirmaciones.1.replic: Ziggurats are solid mud-brick terraces with a temple on top, from the late 3rd millennium BC onward (the one at Ur was built by Ur-Nammu). The foundation inscriptions name their human builders, and the Enuma Elish itself (VI) describes how the bricks of the Esagila and its ziggurat Etemenanki are made. Their form derives from temples on ever higher platforms, as at Eridu and Uruk.
a.entradas.zigurat.afirmaciones.1.fuente: Heiser, sitchiniswrong.com; Jason Colavito, "Damn those lying ancient texts", jasoncolavito.com
a.entradas.zigurat.veredicto: Ziggurats are temple-mountains well documented in archaeology and in building texts; reading them as aerospace installations rests on mistaken etymologies.
